This is the story of how the Bodhisatta (the future Buddha) achieved his first great victory, winning over the evil king Māra. This victory was achieved using his great psychic power, wisdom, and perfections (Pāramīs).
The Vow of Enlightenment
The Bodhisatta, Prince Siddhartha, was ready to become the Buddha. On the evening of the full moon of Kasone, he took eight handfuls of grass (given by Sottiya the grass cutter), which immediately turned into a magnificent Jewel Throne (Ratana Pallaṅka). He sat on this throne, facing east, making a strong promise (a resolve or dhiṭṭhān) that he would not move from this posture until he reached enlightenment. This spot is famously known as the Aparājita Pallaṅka, or the Unconquerable Seat.
Māra's Motivation and Attack
Māra is known as the supreme troublemaker. He is the ruler of the realms of sensual desire (Kāma Loka). Māra was distressed because if the Bodhisatta became the Buddha, many beings would escape his control and the cycle of suffering (saṃsāra).
Māra gathered his countless army and rode the large elephant Girimekhala, displaying a thousand arms holding various weapons. When Māra arrived at the Bodhi Tree, all the surrounding gods, Devas, and Brahmās fled in fear, leaving the Bodhisatta alone.
The Power of Pāramī and Mettā
The Bodhisatta sat fearlessly, relying on the 10 Perfections (Pāramīs) he had accumulated over countless lives. Māra first tried to destroy him with a massive, fierce wind (Vērambha wind) and heavy rain. However, because of the Bodhisatta's immense merit, the wind could not even move his robe, and the rain could not even wet it. Māra then threw every kind of weapon imaginable: stones, fire embers, sand, and spinning blades. The Bodhisatta countered all these threats with the tremendous power of his Loving-kindness (Mettā).
When Māra charged with Girimekhala, the elephant recognized the power of Mettā Pāramī. It refused to attack, instead kneeling down before the Bodhisatta.
The Witness
Māra, humiliated, tried to claim the throne by force, saying it belonged only to him. The Bodhisatta replied calmly, reminding Māra that he had never fulfilled the 10 Pāramīs. The Bodhisatta then called upon a witness to prove his right to the throne: the Earth. As he pointed his finger toward the ground, the Earth, which is 240,000 yojanas thick, rotated and roared like thunder, confirming his acts of merit and charity.
Māra was overcome by fright. He abandoned his thousand weapons and his victory banner, fleeing back to his heaven, followed by his scattered army. This triumph over Māra began the Buddha's conquest of the world.

The story of the Buddha’s victory over Māra is the first of the Eight Outer Victories (Aung Chin Shit Pa), defined as triumphs over external beings or individuals visible with the physical eye, achieved through the Buddha’s exceptional power, wisdom, and perfections (Pāramīs).
Preparation and the Unconquerable Seat
The Bodhisatta, Gautama Buddha, had cultivated the 10 Perfections for the vast period of four asaṅkhyeyyas and 100,000 kappas. On the evening of the Kasone full moon, while sitting under the Mahābodhi tree, the eight handfuls of grass offered by Sottiya the grass cutter transformed into a spectacular 14-cubit Jewel Throne (Ratana Pallaṅka). The Bodhisatta sat facing east, firmly vowing that he would not rise from this position until he achieved Buddhahood, even if his flesh and blood dried up. This resolved posture and the seat itself are known as the Aparājita Pallaṅka, the Unconquerable Seat. This seat was unconquerable because the Bodhisatta, throughout his previous existences, had never knowingly caused anyone to be unjustly moved from their rightful place or honor.
Māra’s Motivation and Arrival
Māra is the "destroyer and hinderer". He possesses the power to dominate the 11 realms of sensual pleasure (Kāma Lokas). Mara was deeply distressed and filled with anxiety when he realized that the Bodhisatta was on the verge of enlightenment, fearing that if the Dharma was preached, beings would escape his domain and attain freedom from the cycle of suffering (saṃsāra).
Leading an immense, uncountable army, Māra advanced from his residence in Vasavattī Heaven to the Bodhi tree. He rode the fierce war elephant Girimekhala and magically manifested a thousand arms, each holding a different weapon. Upon his arrival, the deities, Sakka (Indra), and Brahmās who were worshiping the Bodhisatta fled, only sending him good wishes. The Bodhisatta, however, sat alone and fearless before the terrifying host.
The Elemental and Weapon Attacks
Māra’s army was unable to approach the Bodhisatta, much like flies cannot approach a glowing hot iron ball. Māra first attempted to dislodge the Bodhisatta using verbal threats. Then he summoned the powerful Vērambha wind, strong enough to split mountain peaks and pulverize villages, but when it reached the Bodhisatta, it failed to even rustle the corner of his robe. Next, heavy rains were summoned, but the water failed to wet the Bodhisatta's robe even to the size of a dewdrop. Finally, Māra unleashed torrents of stones, weapons, sand, fire embers, darkness, and spinning weapons. The Bodhisatta successfully pacified all these dreadful threats purely through the power of his accumulated Loving-kindness (Mettā) Pāramī.
The Earth Witness
When Māra personally charged with the elephant Girimekhala, the elephant, overwhelmed by the Mettā Pāramī, was subdued and knelt down, head bowed, before the Bodhisatta. Māra then fell to the ground, shamed. Claiming that the throne belonged only to him, he challenged the Bodhisatta. The Bodhisatta gently countered, asking Māra what witness he could produce to prove he had fulfilled the 10 Pāramīs. When Māra pointed to his vast army as his witness, the Bodhisatta declared that he had no human or divine witnesses, but that the Earth (Vasundharā or Pamsuthīla) would testify to his accumulated charity (Dāna).
As the Bodhisatta pointed his finger to the ground, the great Earth, two hundred and forty thousand yojanas thick, spun like a potter’s wheel and roared loudly like thunder, confirming the merit of his Pāramīs. Māra was instantly seized by immense terror, dropped his thousand weapons, and fled in panic back to Vasavattī Heaven. This magnificent victory over the primary opposing force of the spiritual path was the beginning of the Buddha's conquest of the entire world.

On the full moon evening of Kasone, under the Mahābodhi tree, the eight handfuls of grass offered by the grass cutter Sottiya transformed into the miraculous Ratana Pallaṅka (Jewel Throne). Sitting upon it and leaning against the tree, he made an unshakable vow (dhiṭṭhān): he would not break his cross-legged posture until he achieved Buddhahood, even if his flesh, blood, and bones withered away. This posture and the seat itself became known as the Aparājita Pallaṅka, the Unconquerable Seat. It was unconquerable because the Bodhisatta’s good will (cetanā) in previous lives ensured he never unjustly removed anyone from their rightful status or position.

As the Bodhisatta prepared for the final realization, Māra, known as the cosmic hinderer and destroyer, arrived to interfere. Māra rules the 11 realms of sensual pleasure (Kāma Lokas) and vehemently desired that no being should escape his domain (saṃsāra). Knowing the imminent liberation of countless beings, Māra was overwhelmed by deep distress (sōka hlai pho byāpā po).
Māra marshaled his innumerable army, riding the powerful war elephant Girimekhala, and creating the illusion of a thousand arms wielding various weapons. As the vast army approached the Bodhi Maṇḍa (the area around the tree), the attending Brahmās, Sakka, and Devas instantly fled, only managing to send him thoughts of loving-kindness. The Bodhisatta remained utterly composed and fearless, sitting alone amidst the menacing host.
The Assault and Defense
Mara's forces could not close the distance to the Bodhisatta, akin to swarms of flies unable to approach a glowing iron mass. Māra first attempted to dislodge him through verbal intimidation. Failing that, he escalated to magical and elemental attacks. He unleashed the devastating Vērambha wind, an energy capable of splitting mountains and grinding villages to dust; yet, upon reaching the Bodhisatta, it could not disturb even the fringe of his robe. Next came a torrential rain designed to drown him, but the water failed to wet his robe, not even to the extent of a dewdrop.
Māra followed this with barrages of deadly missiles, including rains of stones, weapons, sand, fire embers, darkness, and spinning weapons. The Bodhisatta’s only countermeasure was the overwhelming force of his accumulated Mettā Pāramī (Perfection of Loving-kindness), which neutralized all these terrifying threats. When Māra charged on Girimekhala, the mighty elephant itself was affected by the Mettā, refusing to harm the Bodhisatta and instead kneeling down in submission.
The Earth as Witness (The Testimony of Dāna)
Fallen from his elephant and filled with shame, Māra challenged the Bodhisatta's claim to the throne: "Siddhartha, arise! This throne belongs solely to me, the powerful one!". The Bodhisatta calmly replied that only he had truly fulfilled the 10 Perfections. When Māra asked for a witness, citing his own massive army, the Bodhisatta proclaimed that the Earth (Pamsuthīla or Vasundharā) would be his witness to the countless acts of charity (Dāna) he had performed.

formattedContent.explorer:
This is the story of the second of the Buddha’s **Eight Outer Victories**: the taming of the fierce **Āḷavaka the Ogre**.

***

The Ogre’s Rule

**Āḷavaka** was a powerful, tough **Ogre** (*Yakkha*), who lived in a grand mansion near a large banyan tree outside the city of **Āḷavī**.

*   Āḷavaka's special rule was to eat anyone who wandered into the shade of his tree around noon.
*   When the **King of Āḷavī** was captured, he promised the Ogre **one person and one pot of rice** every day to save his life.

This terrible practice lasted for **twelve years**. The Ogre ate many people, including criminals, those framed as thieves, and eventually, small **newborn babies**.

***

The Buddha's Visit and the Battle of Patience

One evening, the Buddha visited Āḷavaka's mansion to save the city and convert the Ogre. While the Ogre was away at a meeting of the gods, the Buddha entered the invisible mansion and sat on **Āḷavaka’s royal throne** (*Rāja Pallaṅka*).

Furious upon seeing the Buddha on his special seat, **Āḷavaka** tried to scare him away using:

*   A massive wind and heavy rain.
*   Many physical weapons.
*   His strongest weapon, a terrible white cloth.

The Buddha’s great power made the wind and rain **harmless**. The Ogre’s mighty weapon fell down at the Buddha’s feet like a soft, useless **foot-wiping cloth**.

***

The Power of Words

Since fighting failed, the Ogre roared at the Buddha three times, telling him to leave.

1.  The Buddha quietly left the mansion.
2.  He then calmly went back in when the Ogre told him to return.

This back-and-forth happened three times, which helped cool down the Ogre’s raging anger (*dōsa*).

Finally, the Ogre asked the Buddha a series of **difficult questions**—riddles about life and happiness. The Buddha answered every question perfectly.

Upon hearing the Buddha’s gentle and wise words, the fierce **Āḷavaka** became completely peaceful and accepted the Buddha’s teachings. The Buddha won this victory not with strength or weapons, but with immense **patience** (**forbearance**) and skillful taming.
formattedContent.adventurer:
The defeat of **Āḷavaka the Ogre** (Yakkha) is the Buddha’s second famous conquest, defined as an **Outer Victory** achieved through the power of **wisdom and forbearance**.

The Tragedy of Āḷavī

- **Āḷavaka** was a mighty Ogre living in a hidden mansion near a large banyan tree outside the city of Āḷavī.
- Due to a pact with the **Cātumahārājika devas** (celestial kings), Āḷavaka had the right to seize and devour any living creature that entered his shadow at noon.
- After the King of Āḷavī promised a daily human sacrifice, the city suffered **twelve years of tragedy**.
- The sacrifices, commanded by the desperate King, included:
    1. Criminals
    2. Framed individuals
    3. Newborn infants (when no others could be found)

The Buddha's Intervention

On the morning before the King’s own son, **Prince Āḷavaka Kumāra**, was due to be sent, the Buddha used his divine vision (*Sabbeññutañāṇa Cakkhu*).

He foresaw that his intervention would lead to great spiritual benefits:
- The Prince would attain **Anāgāmi fruition**.
- The Ogre would attain **Sotāpatti fruition** (initial stages of enlightenment).

The Buddha traveled alone to the Ogre’s invisible mansion that very evening. He entered the premises and sat fearlessly on the Ogre’s **Rāja Pallaṅka** (royal throne).

When Āḷavaka returned from a celestial meeting and saw the Buddha on his seat, he was overcome with intense rage (**Dōsa**).

The Failure of Force

Āḷavaka used all his immense powers to attack:
- He summoned mountain-splitting winds and heavy rains.
- He launched a barrage of weapons, including stones and fire.
- He threw his most potent weapon—a fierce **white cloth weapon** that could supposedly set the ocean aflame.

Due to the Buddha's overwhelming spiritual power, this fearsome weapon was instantly pacified, falling uselessly at his feet like a piece of foot-wiping cloth.

Taming Through Technique

Defeated by power, the Ogre resorted to intimidation, shouting at the Buddha to leave.

To pacify the Ogre’s violent mind, the Buddha practiced a mental technique: he peacefully exited the mansion when ordered, and re-entered when ordered. This three-time repetition of entering and exiting was done deliberately by the Buddha to reduce the Ogre’s anger and make him receptive to the **Dharma**.

Once calmed, Āḷavaka, impressed by the Buddha’s wisdom and control, challenged him with deep, ancient questions (*Pyassana*) that his parents had learned from **Kassapa Buddha** and inscribed on a gold plate.

The Buddha answered flawlessly, explaining that:
- The best wealth is **Saddhā** (faith).
- The best practice is the **10 virtuous deeds (Kusala)** (Dāna, Sīla, Bhāvanā).
- The greatest flavor is **truthful speech (Satta Vacana)**.

Hearing these profound truths, the tough, relentless Ogre instantly attained **Sotāpatti fruition**. The Ogre had been tamed not by force, but by **profound patience and skillful wisdom**. The Buddha then led the converted Ogre into Āḷavī city for alms, marking the successful conquest.
formattedContent.storyteller:
This is the story of the Buddha’s **second great victory**. It is the story of how he won over a very scary, bad giant named **Āḷavaka**.

### The Scary Giant

**Āḷavaka the Ogre** was a powerful giant who lived near a big tree in a city called Āḷavī.

*   He had permission to eat anyone who came near his tree's shadow during the day.
*   The King of Āḷavī was caught by the Ogre and promised to send the giant **one person every single day** to eat, so the King could be freed.
*   This went on for **12 long years**, and many people were eaten.

### The Buddha Visits

When almost all the people were gone, the **Buddha decided to help**.

1.  The Buddha went straight to Āḷavaka’s house (a mansion) near the big tree.
2.  The Ogre was away, so the Buddha quietly went inside and sat down on the Ogre’s **special throne**.
3.  When Āḷavaka came home, he became extremely angry. He threw big winds, strong rain, and all kinds of scary weapons, like stones and fire.
4.  The Ogre even threw his best weapon, a white cloth weapon. But because of the Buddha’s **huge kindness and power**, all the weapons disappeared!
5.  The special white cloth just fell harmlessly at the Buddha’s feet like a *soft towel*.

### The Best Answers

When Āḷavaka could not win by fighting, he decided to ask the Buddha **tricky questions**. The Buddha gave wise, gentle, and perfect answers.

The Ogre learned:

*   **Faith (trust)** is the best treasure.
*   **Being truthful** is the best flavor.

Because of the Buddha’s wisdom and patience, the tough and angry Āḷavaka became **good and peaceful** right away. The Buddha won without any fighting!
formattedContent.voyager:
The conquest of **Āḷavaka the Ogre** (*Yakkha*) represents the Buddha’s **Second Outer Victory** (*Aung Chin Shit Pa*). This victory, achieved in the city of Āḷavī, demonstrates the supreme efficacy of **Khandī** (Patience) and **Sūdanta** (Skillful Taming).

***

### The Ogre's Dominion and the King's Covenant

**Āḷavaka** was an exceptionally fierce Ogre who dwelled in a majestic, hidden mansion near a banyan tree outside Āḷavī. He operated under a granted license from the **Cātumahārājika devas**, permitting him to seize and consume any being entering the tree’s shadow around noon.

When the King of Āḷavī trespassed into this fatal zone, he was forced into a desperate, secret covenant: he would send the Ogre one human victim and one meal pot daily. This tragic arrangement continued for twelve years, leading the Minister to sacrifice all criminals, framed individuals, and eventually, every newborn infant in the city.

### The Buddha's Divine Intervention

Anticipating the sacrifice of the last remaining infant, **Prince Āḷavaka Kumāra**, the Buddha used his omniscience (*Sabbeññutañāṇa Cakkhu*) to observe the world. He saw that this intervention would lead to the Prince achieving **Anāgāmi fruition** and, crucially, the Ogre achieving **Sotāpatti fruition**.

The Buddha traveled alone to the Ogre’s realm, and finding the Ogre absent, he entered the mansion and sat on the **Rāja Pallaṅka** (Royal Throne). Upon his return from the celestial assembly, Āḷavaka was "furious" and "overflowing with rage" upon seeing the tranquil Buddha seated on his personal throne.

### The Defeat of Physical Force

Āḷavaka first employed elemental attacks, unleashing a **Vērambha wind** powerful enough to split mountains, and torrential rain, neither of which could disturb the Buddha’s robe. He then hurled a barrage of weapons.

His final, most formidable weapon was the **white cloth weapon** (*Bwut Phyu Pusoe Laknet*)—said to possess the power to ignite the ocean. However, against the Buddha’s profound spiritual momentum, this weapon was instantaneously defused, dropping harmlessly to the ground near the Buddha's feet, resembling a mere **foot-wiping cloth** (*Che Thote Pusoe*).

### The Victory of Patience and Wisdom

Defeated physically, Āḷavaka resorted to mental harassment, shouting fiercely at the Buddha to leave. The Buddha deliberately employed a psychological tactic: he would peacefully exit when commanded and re-enter when commanded, performing this exchange three times. This intentional repetition was used to check the Ogre’s escalating rage (**Dōsa**) and to cultivate a temporary state of mental tranquility, making him susceptible to the Dharma.

The Ogre then attempted to defeat the Buddha intellectually by posing a set of profound questions (**Pyassana**) concerning life, wealth, happiness, and morality, which were ancient wisdom inherited from his parents who learned them from **Kassapa Buddha**.

The Buddha answered them precisely:

1.  Supreme wealth is **Saddhā** (unshakeable faith in the Triple Gem).
2.  The practice that brings happiness is **Kusala 10** (good deeds, including *Dāna*, *Sīla*, and *Bhāvanā*).
3.  The best flavor is **Satta Vacana** (truthful speech).
4.  The noblest livelihood is one supported by **Paññā** (wisdom).

He further explained that one crosses the current of *saṃsāra* (the cycle of rebirth) with **Saddhā**, transcends suffering with diligence in **Kusala** and the 10 Perfections (**Pāramīs**), and purifies defilements (*Kilēsa*) with **Vipassanā Paññā** (insight wisdom).

Having his ancient, inscribed questions answered perfectly, the Ogre, who was inherently virtuous due to previous merit, immediately attained **Sotāpatti fruition**. The Ogre had become well-tamed (**Sūdanta**).

The next morning, the Ogre, now a stream-enterer, received the infant Prince, gently presented him to the Buddha, and dedicated him to the Triple Gem. The Prince, renamed **Hatthāḷavaka** (referring to being passed from hand-to-hand), later became distinguished among the Buddha’s lay disciples for his skill in supporting his followers (*Pārisasaṅgaṇhaṇta*). The successful taming of this immensely fierce Ogre, achieved through the Buddha's boundless **Patience**, became the **Second Great Victory**.

***

*Analogy:* The taming of Āḷavaka is like a master jeweler handling a diamond rough. Instead of crushing the stone with overwhelming force (which would be useless, as seen when the physical weapons failed), the Buddha patiently applied subtle pressure (the three-time exit/entry) and then polished the stone with the precise tool of truth (answering the *Pyassana*), revealing the inherent light (**Sotāpatti realization**) within the fiercely tempered Ogre.

formattedContent.voyager:
The victory over **Nāḷāgiri**, known as the **Third Outer Victory**, exemplifies the Buddha's supreme spiritual authority, demonstrating the absolute power of **Mettā Pāramī** (the Perfection of Loving-kindness) to overcome extreme malice and brute force. The conquest was achieved by "sprinkling the water of loving-kindness" (*Mettāmbuseka*).

The event occurred during the Buddha's **20th Rains Retreat** in Rājagaha. Devadatta, whose deep-seated hatred (*āghaṭa*) for the Buddha had intensified, decided to employ the brute force of the powerful royal elephant, Nāḷāgiri.

Devadatta instructed the elephant keepers to double the elephant’s customary intake of alcohol, administering **16 pots of strong liquor**.

This act of chemical and mental provocation transformed the elephant into an engine of destruction, rendered "extremely intoxicated" (*ati-maddabhūta*), and terrifyingly fierce, comparable to a forest fire, a destructive wheel, or a thunderbolt. The keepers boasted that the Buddha's life would soon hang from the elephant's tusks.

The Moment of Confrontation

The next morning, the Buddha, surrounded by the Sangha, entered Rājagaha for his alms round. **Nāḷāgiri** was released and charged at the Buddha, trumpeting loudly and rapidly, aiming to crush him.

The event created profound tension.

- Venerable **Sāriputta** and **Moggallāna** begged the Buddha to permit them to handle the fierce animal or to choose a different route, but the Buddha refused.
- In a display of ultimate devotion, Venerable **Ānanda** positioned himself directly in front of the Buddha, prepared to sacrifice his life, until the Buddha instructed him to move.

The Buddha stood alone and unwavering. He deployed the immense spiritual power he had accumulated across countless *kappas* through his perfections. He projected the full, potent force of his **Mettā Pāramī**. The Buddha also addressed Nāḷāgiri directly, calling him by name and commanding him to approach, pointing out that he was sent to kill the Buddha specifically.

The Taming and Conversion

Hearing the Buddha’s words and instantly receiving the overwhelming energy of *Mettā*, the elephant’s drunken frenzy vanished, and it recovered its senses (*sati*).

The ferocious animal was instantly pacified:

1.  It lowered its trunk, its tail, and its ears.
2.  It knelt down (*Ngup sin dop pyap*) at the Buddha's feet.

The Buddha gently touched the elephant's head and delivered a discourse (*dhamma*). He emphasized that acts of violence lead to long-term suffering in the lower realms, whereas cultivating **Mettā** brings happiness and safety. Filled with **Saddhā** (faith), the tamed elephant took refuge in the Triple Gem and observed the Five Precepts.

The citizens, watching from their homes, were overwhelmed with joy and awe. They showered the tamed elephant with the seven kinds of jewels. Since the elephant’s body became covered in this wealth, it was subsequently known as **Dhanapāla** (Guardian of Wealth). The audience who witnessed this miracle also attained spiritual insight. Nāḷāgiri never again displayed aggression, remaining docile and well-tamed.

This victory demonstrated that **Mettā** is the ultimate, non-violent conqueror, neutralizing the most extreme forms of malice and physical aggression. It is a powerful example of spiritual mastery prevailing over destructive material force.

**Analogy for Understanding:**

The Buddha's victory over Nāḷāgiri is like using a powerful fire extinguisher to put out a huge gasoline fire. Devadatta fueled the elephant with alcohol to make it a weapon of pure, raging combustion (the fire/thunderbolt), but the Buddha’s *Mettā* acted as a boundless, cooling deluge of water, instantly extinguishing the aggression and leaving only peace and calm behind.

*   In a moment of immense devotion, Venerable **Ānanda** stepped in front of the Buddha, declaring he would rather die himself than allow the Buddha to be harmed, before the Buddha bade him stand aside.

- Its clear consciousness (*sati*) returned.
- The fierce animal was pacified, lowering its tail, ears, and trunk.
- It then knelt down (*Ngup sin dop pyap*) directly before the Buddha’s feet.

Renaming and Result

The elephant, now tamed, was filled with faith (**Saddhā**) and took the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts.

The Rājagaha citizens, who had watched the terrifying event, cheered and praised the Buddha. They showered the elephant with the seven kinds of jewels (gold, silver, etc.). Because its entire body was covered by the wealth strewn upon it, Nāḷāgiri was permanently renamed **Dhanapāla** (**Guardian of Wealth**). Through this act of sublime non-violence, the Buddha conquered aggression and malice.

The conquest of Aṅgulimāla is the fourth of the Eight Outer Victories, illustrating the Buddha's ability to tame the most ruthless aggression using profound wisdom and psychic power (Iddhī).
The Cursed Name and the Evil Deed
Aṅgulimāla was born in Sāvatthi as Ahimsaka, the son of the King’s chief priest, Bhaggava, and his wife Mantāṇī. At his birth, the stars indicated a thief, and the weapons in the city glowed. Although the King was advised that the child would only be a lone thief, the parents named him Ahimsaka ("Harmless").
Ahiṃsaka studied diligently at Takkasilā. However, jealousy from other students led them to falsely accuse him of seducing the teacher's wife. The wicked teacher, unable to kill his student directly, devised a subtle death plot: he demanded that Ahiṃsaka bring him one thousand human fingers (pūjā) as the price for his entire education. Ahiṃsaka, still obedient, began his killing spree, acquiring the infamous name Aṅgulimāla (Finger Garland) after stringing the cut fingers around his neck.
The Buddha’s Merciful Intervention
After terrorizing the kingdom, Aṅgulimāla had killed 999 people. King Pasenadi of Kosala prepared 500 horsemen to capture him. Aṅgulimāla’s devoted mother, Mantāṇī, set out alone to warn her son.
The Buddha foresaw that Aṅgulimāla was on the verge of killing his own mother—an act of severe kamma that would have locked him in Avīci Hell (saṃsāra dukkha); however, the Buddha also saw his potential for enlightenment. To prevent the matricide and save the Ogre, the Buddha walked alone into the forest, positioning himself between Aṅgulimāla and his mother.
Aṅgulimāla spotted the Buddha and rushed to kill him, chasing him for three yojanas. Despite Aṅgulimāla running full speed, the Buddha used his great psychic power (Iddhī) to make the ground and distance seem endless.
The Victory of Truth
Exhausted, Aṅgulimāla shouted, "Stop, Monk! Stop!". The Buddha calmly replied: "Aṅgulimāla, I have stopped. You alone have not stopped".
Aṅgulimāla challenged the Buddha, accusing him of lying (a musāvāda). The Buddha explained that true stopping means abstaining from all harmful deeds (Paṇātipāta duscarit) and establishing oneself in the supreme happiness of Nirvāṇa (Sugati). Aṅgulimāla, however, was still rooted in violent deeds and had not stopped traveling the path of suffering.
Hearing this profound truth from the fearless Buddha, Aṅgulimāla was instantly humbled. He flung his weapons and the garland of fingers into a ravine. The Buddha ordained him instantly with the phrase "Ehi Bhikkhu Sampadā", and Aṅgulimāla transformed into a peaceful monk. This conquest was a demonstration of winning by truth and skillful taming, rather than by physical confrontation.

Acting out of supreme compassion, the Buddha intercepted Aṅgulimāla.
Aṅgulimāla decided to take the monk's life for his final finger. He drew his weapon and pursued the Buddha with relentless speed across a distance of three yojanas. However, the Buddha, using his psychic power (Iddhī), traversed the terrain (including ravines and water) while simultaneously making the distance feel infinite to the sprinting thief.
The Discourse of True Cessation
Utterly exhausted, Aṅgulimāla shouted, "Stop, Monk! Stop!".
The Buddha, standing firm, replied: "Aṅgulimāla, I have stopped. You alone have not stopped".
Aṅgulimāla challenged the Buddha, questioning how the moving monk could claim to have stopped while the stationary thief had not. The Buddha explained that he had ceased all forms of malice, harassment, and moral defilements (duscarit). The conquest of **Ciñcamāṇavikā** (The Wicked Woman) is the Buddha’s **Fifth Outer Victory**, achieved through non-violent means known as the *Sānta Sōma Vidhinā* (**calm, pure, and peaceful technique**). This episode highlights the failure of malicious slander against spiritual purity and the certainty of **immediate karmic retribution**.

***

### The Conspiracy of Envy

The event occurred while the Buddha was residing at the **Jetavana Monastery** following his seventh *Vassa* (Rains Retreat) in Tāvatiṃsa Heaven.

The Buddha's immense popularity led to a vast increase in followers and accrued offerings (*Lābhsappakāra*). Rival religious leaders (**Tirthikas**) saw their own influence and material support dwindle, likening their obscurity to glowworms fading upon the sunrise.

Motivated by intense jealousy (*Wunto Sit*), they sought to undermine the Buddha's moral standing. They enlisted **Ciñcamāṇavikā**, a beautiful, youthful, and cunning *Paribbājikā* (female wanderer), to execute the character assassination.

***

### The Deliberate Campaign of Deception

Ciñcamāṇavikā accepted the charge to damage the Buddha's reputation and dry up his offerings. She implemented a **long-term strategy**:

1.  **Vague Insignuation:** For approximately a month, she walked toward **Jetavana** in the evening and returned in the morning from the direction of the monastery, maintaining the illusion of a secret tryst.
2.  **Explicit Claim:** After this initial phase, she claimed explicitly to have been sleeping with the Buddha in the **Gandhakūṭi Vihāra**.
3.  **The Fabrication:** Following eight or nine months, she secured a duck-egg-shaped wooden knob (*Bē u ta kyan Hpō thit thā Hpū*) to her abdomen using internal ropes or straps, concealing the structure under a red garment to simulate a full-term pregnancy. She also bruised her hands and feet with a cow bone (*Nwa mē Yō*) to create **artificial swelling**, completing the illusion of late-term physical strain.

***

### The Lion’s Roar and Divine Intervention

She confronted the Buddha while he was seated on the *Buddhasana Dhamma Pallaṅka*, delivering a sermon to a large, attentive congregation. She stood directly before him and launched a fierce, public accusation, claiming he only cared for pleasure (*Mweelyaw Pyaw Hpō*) and urging him to build a lying-in house or instruct his patrons to care for the "child" she bore by him.

The Buddha paused his sermon and responded with the fearless authority of a **Lion's Roar**:
"Sister Ciñcamāṇā, whether what you say is true or false, **only you and I know**."

She defiantly reasserted her claim.

At that critical moment, **Sakka** (Indra), perceiving the injustice, descended to the assembly with four **Devas**.

*   These Devas manifested as **rats**.
*   They collectively gnawed through the ropes binding the wooden knob.
*   A simultaneous gust of wind blew her outer garment upwards, and the wooden device fell, shattering onto her feet and **breaking both of them**.

***

### Karmic Retribution

The enraged assembly realized they had been deceived. They cursed and attacked **Ciñcamāṇā** with sticks and stones, driving her out of the monastery.

Crucially, as soon as she was outside the Buddha's protective gaze, the **Earth opened up** (*Myē myui hat*). She was immediately engulfed by flames from the lowest hell and dragged down to **Avīci Hell**.

This swift and terrifying **karmic retribution** confirmed the moral purity of the Buddha and solidified the **Fifth Great Victory**.

***

### Analogy for Understanding

This victory is like a forged check being presented to a bank CEO. Ciñcamāṇā presented a perfect, months-long fabrication (the forged check/fake pregnancy) to the public. The Buddha, the spiritual authority, simply stated the truth ("Only you and I know"), and the **cosmic forces** (Sakka and the rats) acted as an audit, instantly proving the forgery, leading to the immediate and irreversible punishment of the fraudster.

***

### The Jealous Friends

The Buddha had many, many followers, and everyone gave him food and gifts. Because of this, some other teachers, called the **Tirthikas**, became very jealous and lost their own followers and gifts.

They hired a beautiful, but bad, woman named **Ciñcamāṇā** to make up lies about the Buddha. Her job was to make people stop believing in the Buddha.

### The Big Lie

Ciñcamāṇā pretended she was going to have the Buddha’s baby.

1.  For many months, she wrapped herself in cloth and even tied a wooden piece (**Kaṭṭhamudaram**) to her tummy to make it look like she was heavily pregnant.
2.  One day, while the Buddha was teaching a big crowd, Ciñcamāṇā stood right in front of him and yelled, saying he was a bad father and asking him to build a house for the baby.

### The Magic Happens

The Buddha just looked at her calmly and said, **"Sister Ciñcamāṇā, whether what you say is true or false, only you and I know."**

*   Suddenly, the great God **Sakka** (*Indra*) knew the woman was lying.
*   Sakka sent tiny helper gods who looked like small rats.
*   These rats chewed the strings holding the wooden piece. The wood fell down onto Ciñcamāṇā’s feet and **broke both of them**.
*   Everyone saw the big lie!

The crowd chased her away. As soon as she was out of the Buddha's sight, the **Earth opened up and swallowed her**, dragging her down to the lowest hell. The Buddha won by being perfectly **calm and truthful**.

They tasked the beautiful and charismatic female wanderer (**Paribbājikā**), **Ciñcamāṇā**, to orchestrate the Buddha's public downfall.

1.  For nearly a month, she entered the monastery grounds in the evening, pretending to spend the night there, and then exiting in the morning. She gave intentionally ambiguous answers to anyone who asked where she had spent the night.
2.  After about four months, she escalated the lie, claiming explicitly to have spent the night with the Buddha in the **Gandhakūṭi Vihāra**.
3.  After eight or nine months, she progressed to the final stage of deceit:
    *   She tied a **duck-egg-shaped wooden knob** (*Bē u ta kyan Hpō thit thā Hpū*) to her belly with ropes and wrapped it in cloth, giving the appearance of late-stage pregnancy.
    *   She bruised her hands and feet with a **cow bone** (*Nwa mē Yō*) to simulate the swelling of advanced gestation.

She confronted the Buddha while he was seated on the **Buddhasana Dhamma Pallaṅka**, delivering a discourse to a vast assembly. She accused him of being immoral, claiming he was only concerned with spiritual pleasure (*Mweelyaw Pyaw Hpō*) while neglecting his supposed unborn son, demanding he fulfill the duties of a father.

At that moment, **Sakka** (Indra), realizing the injustice, descended with four Devas. They took the form of rats and simultaneously gnawed through the cords securing the wooden knob. A sudden gust of wind lifted her outer garment. The wooden knob fell, shattering onto her feet and breaking both of them.

The assembled crowd, seeing the undeniable proof of her fabrication, became enraged. They insulted her and chased her out of the monastery using sticks and stones. Just as she passed out of the Buddha's sight, the Earth opened up, and she was dragged down by flames into **Avīci Hell**. This is the **Sixth Outer Victory**, where the Buddha defeated **Saccaka the Wanderer** using only his powerful **wisdom** (*Paññā*).

**The Arrogant Teacher**

Saccaka was a well-known teacher in Vesālī who had mastered a thousand different philosophies and teachings (*Vādas*). He was extremely **arrogant**.

He was so proud of his huge amount of knowledge that he genuinely feared his stomach might burst open like an overfilled rice sack. To prevent this painful embarrassment, he wrapped an **iron plate** around his stomach.

Saccaka was a follower of a group called the **Nigaṇṭhas**. He strongly disagreed with the Buddha’s teachings, especially the idea that the body (*Rūpa*) is **impermanent** (*Anicca*) and is **non-self** (*Anatta*). The victory over **Saccaka the Wanderer** (also referred to as **Kūṭadanta**) is the **Sixth Outer Victory**, a profound triumph over philosophical **dogmatism** and intellectual pride, achieved solely through the clarity of **Paññā** (wisdom).

***

### The Nigaṇṭha Background and Intellectual Arrogance

*   Saccaka was a prominent **Nigaṇṭha** (Jain) **Paribbājaka** (wanderer) residing in Vesālī.
*   His educational background was legendary: he mastered the **1,000 Vādas** (philosophical discourses)—500 taught by his father and 500 by his mother.
*   He was highly influential, serving as a teacher to the Licchavī princes.
*   Saccaka’s defining trait was extreme **intellectual arrogance**. He sincerely believed that the volume of knowledge he contained could not be safely held, imagining his stomach would burst like an overfilled sack of grain.
*   To counter this presumed physical risk, he wore an **iron plate** tightly wrapped around his abdomen.

***

### The Clash: The Doctrine of Anattā

Saccaka sought to challenge the Buddha's core teaching that all conditioned phenomena, especially the **Five Aggregates** (Rūpa, Vedanā, Saññā, Saṅkhāra, Viññāṇa), are defined by the three characteristics: impermanence (**Anicca**), suffering (**Dukkha**), and non-self (**Anattā**).

Saccaka insisted that the body (**Rūpa**) was the definitive **Atta** (self).

The Buddha, knowing Saccaka’s pride stemmed from his false view (**Diṭṭhi**), chose to bypass abstract theory and challenge the practical reality of Saccaka's claim to mastery over his body.

***

### The Crucial Question of Control

1.  The Buddha asked Saccaka: "If you claim that the **Rūpa** (physical body) is your self, you must, by definition, be the sovereign master of it. Does your *Rūpa* submit to your will?"
2.  The Buddha then pressed the matter by asking if Saccaka could command his body to remain perpetually beautiful, unblemished by aging, and fixed at the youthful age of sixteen, simply by wishing it so.
3.  The Buddha was probing the inherent lack of control over the body’s natural process of decay, a manifestation of **Anattā**.
4.  Saccaka was instantly trapped. He realized that if he answered "yes," he would fail the demonstration; if he answered "no," he would affirm the Buddha's doctrine that the body is not subject to his command.
5.  Paralyzed by shame and the realization of his error, Saccaka remained completely silent.

***

### Divine Intervention and Conversion

*   Since Saccaka refused to respond, the powerful god **Sakka** (Indra) appeared, visible only to the Buddha and Saccaka, disguised as a terrifying **Yakkha**.
*   Sakka threatened Saccaka with a **steel mace** (iron club), saying he would strike him if he did not answer the Buddha.
*   Fearing the god's wrath and recognizing the Buddha's immense wisdom and psychic power (**Iddhī**), Saccaka finally broke his silence and confessed: "**Venerable Gotama, I am greatly mistaken**."
*   He then vowed to respect and rely on the Buddha's teachings for the rest of his life.
*   The Buddha’s triumph over Saccaka was achieved by demonstrating that arrogance based on mere learned knowledge is powerless against the practical, self-evident truth realized through **Wisdom**. Saccaka was defeated, his great pride broken, and his adherence to false views overcome.

***

### Analogy

*The debate with Saccaka is like trying to convince a chess master that a pawn (the body) is the most powerful piece on the board (the self).* Saccaka insists, "*I command the pawn!*" The Buddha simply asks, "Can you command the pawn to move backward, or change color, just because you wish it?" The moment Saccaka realizes the pawn is bound by unchangeable rules (impermanence and decay), he understands that despite his knowledge, he is not the ultimate master, and the true nature of the body (the pawn) is **Anattā**.

3.  **Saññā** (perception)

5.  **Viññāṇa** (consciousness)

-   If he answered "yes," the Licchavī princes watching the debate would demand immediate proof, which he could not provide.
-   If he answered **"no,"** he would have to concede that the *Rūpa* is not subject to his will and therefore must be **Anattā**.

Terrified, Saccaka finally conceded that he was gravely mistaken and confessed his faith in the Buddha.

Thus, the Buddha conquered Saccaka by piercing his **false views** (*Diṭṭhi*) with the sharp light of **Wisdom**.

lessons.title: The story of the Buddha’s victory over Nandōpananda

formattedContent.voyager:
*The conquest of Nandōpananda the Nāga King* is the **Buddha’s Seventh Outer Victory**, an exceptional achievement through the skillful application of **psychic power (Iddhī)** and wisdom. This method is specifically known as the **Iddhūpadēsa Vidhinā** (method of instruction in psychic power).

**The Premise and the Wrong View**

The incident occurred after the Buddha’s tenth **Vassa** (Rains Retreat) in the Pārileya forest. The Buddha, accompanied by **500 Arahants**, was traveling in the sky to receive alms from Anāthapiṇḍika. The Buddha used his omniscience to foresee the fate of Nandōpananda Nāga, who, despite past merits, was currently born as an animal (**Tiracchāna**) and held aggressive **wrong views (Micchā Diṭṭhi)**.

As the Arahants flew through the sky above the Nāga’s magnificent abode, the falling foot-dust from the "bald-headed monks" (**U Pyae Rahans**) enraged Nandōpananda. Driven by malice, the Nāga utilized his colossal power to obstruct the entire route to Tāvatiṃsa Heaven.

He caused the obstruction in two major ways:
-   He wrapped his body **seven times**, coiling around **Mount Meru (Yugandhara Mountain)** from base to peak.
-   His massive hood then covered the vast expanse of the **Tāvatiṃsa Heaven**, rendering it invisible.

**The Selection of the Chief Disciple**

Faced with this immense obstruction, several Arahants offered their services to tame the Nāga, including Rāhula, Bhaddiya, and others. The Buddha gently refused them all, knowing that only a disciple who had perfected the power of the **Four Iddhipādas** (Bases of Psychic Power) could succeed.

**Venerable Mahā Moggallāna**, the Buddha’s chief left-hand disciple and supreme master of **Iddhī**, then volunteered, noting that a chief disciple must bear the burden of his teacher. The Buddha assented, authorizing him to use his formidable power: *"My son Moggallāna, you alone must tame him."*

**The Duel of Psychic Power**

Moggallāna immediately entered the **fourth Jhāna** (meditative absorption). He transformed himself into a Nāga of superior size, power, and splendor.

1.  He coiled his enormous body **14 times** around Nandōpananda, crushing him against the unmoving Mount Meru.
2.  The Nāga King retaliated with ferocious, poison-laced smoke and fire. Moggallāna countered by projecting a superior flame which, unlike the Nāga’s fire, pierced Nandōpananda’s skin and caused him pain and humiliation.
3.  Next, the Nāga opened his gigantic mouth, intending to swallow the monk. Moggallāna entered the mouth and performed a physical promenade (*cankram*) along the length of the Nāga's intestines and stomach.
4.  When the Nāga pleaded with Moggallāna to exit the "filthy" interior, Moggallāna emerged, stood between the Nāga's tusks, and used his psychic foot to strike the tusks before escaping the ensuing snap.

**The Final Submission**

Realizing that Moggallāna's power was absolute, Nandōpananda fled into the water, transforming into a human youth. Moggallāna, demonstrating a higher tier of **Iddhī**, immediately transformed into the majestic, terrifying **Garuda** (the ancient nemesis of the Nāga race) and pursued him.

When the Nāga changed into a human, Moggallāna changed into a fierce **Yakkha** (Ogre) and threatened to consume him, achieving total spiritual dominance.

Defeated in every form and capacity, Nandōpananda humbled himself, confessed his profound error (**Māha Mhā Chē Pyi**), and took refuge in the Buddha. Moggallāna then led the converted Nāga to the Buddha, who instructed him in the Dharma, establishing him as an **Upāsaka** (lay follower). This decisive victory showcased that even beings of great natural power must submit to the pure, trained spiritual force of the Arahant.

### The Angry Giant Snake

The Buddha and 500 monks were traveling high up in the sky to a special place called **Tāvatiṃsa Heaven**. Below them lived a giant snake king named **Nandōpananda**.

Nandōpananda was rich and powerful, but he got very **angry** when dust from the monks’ feet fell onto his head as they flew over. He shouted that he would not let them pass again!

To stop them, the giant *Nāga* snake wrapped his huge body around **Mount Meru**, which is a huge mountain, all the way from the bottom to the top. He then covered the entire sky above with his big snake hood, **blocking the sun and the way to Heaven**.

### The Taming by the Helper

The Buddha told his special helper, Venerable **Moggallāna**, to go tame the angry *Nāga*.

Moggallāna used his special **magic powers (Iddhī)**:

1.  First, he turned into a **Nāga snake** even bigger than Nandōpananda. He wrapped his own huge body around the angry Nāga **14 times**, squeezing him.
2.  The bad Nāga tried to hurt Moggallāna with fire and smoke, but Moggallāna’s fire was **stronger** and hurt the Nāga instead.
3.  Moggallāna then turned himself into a **Garuda bird**—which is the biggest enemy of snakes!

The Nāga king was so scared that he gave up immediately. He changed back into a small, polite boy and bowed at the Buddha’s feet.

The Buddha won the victory because **Moggallāna** was able to use his amazing powers to help the angry snake become good and peaceful.

content.adventurer:
The defeat of Nandōpananda the Nāga King is the Seventh Outer Victory, a pivotal event where the Buddha used Venerable Mahā Moggallāna and his proficiency in psychic power (Iddhī) to conquer a powerful being holding wrong views (Dugāha-Diṭṭhi).
The Nāga's Arrogance and Obstruction
The Buddha and 500 Arahants were flying towards Tāvatiṃsa Heaven, having been invited for alms by Anāthapiṇḍika. The Buddha foresaw that the mighty Nandōpananda Nāga King, despite having good merit (Kusala Puñña), was currently an animal (Tiracchāna) and held obstinate wrong views (Micchā Diṭṭhi).
As the monks flew overhead, dust from their feet fell upon the Nāga's magnificent abode, which Nandōpananda interpreted as a great insult. In a fit of immense rage (Añññakha Dōsa), he vowed to block their passage. He swelled his body to colossal size, wrapped himself 14-fold around Mount Meru (from base to peak), and then used his hood to cover the entirety of Tāvatiṃsa Heaven.
The Chosen Conqueror
The traveling monks found their path blocked. Several elders, including Rāhula and Bhaddiya, requested permission to subdue the Nāga, but the Buddha refused them all.
Finally, Venerable Mahā Moggallāna, renowned as the chief disciple specializing in psychic power, requested the task, stating that a chief disciple must bear the burden of his master. The Buddha granted him permission: "My son Moggallāna, you must tame him". The victory was based on the Buddha's instruction in psychic power (Iddhūpadēsa) given to his son/disciple.
Moggallāna immediately utilized the fourth Jhāna (meditative absorption). He transformed into a Nāga of even greater size and splendor. He coiled his body 14 times around the indignant Nandōpananda and crushed him against the mountain. The Nāga retaliated by emitting poison-laden smoke and flames, but Moggallāna countered with a superior flame that bypassed the Nāga's scales, burning his skin.
Humiliation and Submission
The Nāga then attempted to swallow Moggallāna. Moggallāna entered the Nāga’s mouth and then demonstrated his complete mastery by walking a cankram (meditation promenade) along the length of the Nāga's belly and intestines.
Completely defeated, Nandōpananda tried to flee. Moggallāna transformed into a colossal Garuda (the mythical enemy of Nāgas) and pursued him. Terrified, the Nāga changed into a human youth, and Moggallāna, demonstrating absolute superiority, changed into a giant Yakkha (ogre) and feigned eating him.
Humbled and broken, Nandōpananda submitted, acknowledged his profound error, and took refuge in the Triple Gem, becoming a converted lay follower. This victory was a masterful display of spiritual power conquering arrogance and false views.

Several senior monks, including Rāhula, requested permission to tame the Nāga, but the Buddha refused them. Finally, Venerable Mahā Moggallāna, known for his supreme psychic power, requested permission, affirming his duty as the Buddha’s chief disciple. The Buddha consented.

The conquest of Nandōpananda the Nāga King is the Buddha’s Seventh Outer Victory, an exceptional achievement through the skillful application of psychic power (Iddhī) and wisdom, specifically known as the Iddhūpadēsa Vidhinā (method of instruction in psychic power).
The Premise and the Wrong View
The incident occurred after the Buddha’s tenth Vassa (Rains Retreat) in the Pārileya forest. The Buddha, accompanied by 500 Arahants, was traveling in the sky to receive alms from Anāthapiṇḍika. The Buddha used his omniscience to foresee the fate of Nandōpananda Nāga, who, despite past merits, was currently born as an animal (Tiracchāna) and held aggressive wrong views (Micchā Diṭṭhi).
As the Arahants flew through the sky above the Nāga’s magnificent abode, the falling foot-dust from the "bald-headed monks" (U Pyae Rahans) enraged Nandōpananda. Driven by malice, the Nāga utilized his colossal power to obstruct the entire route to Tāvatiṃsa Heaven. He wrapped his body seven times, coiling around Mount Meru (Yugandhara Mountain) from base to peak. His massive hood then covered the vast expanse of the Tāvatiṃsa Heaven, rendering it invisible.
The Selection of the Chief Disciple
Faced with this immense obstruction, several Arahants offered their services to tame the Nāga, including Rāhula, Bhaddiya, and others. The Buddha gently refused them all, knowing that only a disciple who had perfected the power of the Four Iddhipādas (Bases of Psychic Power) could succeed.
Venerable Mahā Moggallāna, the Buddha’s chief left-hand disciple and supreme master of Iddhī, then volunteered, noting that a chief disciple must bear the burden of his teacher. The Buddha assented, authorizing him to use his formidable power: "My son Moggallāna, you alone must tame him".
The Duel of Psychic Power
Moggallāna immediately entered the fourth Jhāna (meditative absorption). He transformed himself into a Nāga of superior size, power, and splendor. He then coiled his enormous body 14 times around Nandōpananda, crushing him against the unmoving Mount Meru.
The Nāga King retaliated with ferocious, poison-laced smoke and fire. Moggallāna countered by projecting a superior flame which, unlike the Nāga’s fire, pierced Nandōpananda’s skin and caused him pain and humiliation.
Next, the Nāga opened his gigantic mouth, intending to swallow the monk. Moggallāna entered the mouth and performed a physical promenade (cankram) along the length of the Nāga's intestines and stomach. When the Nāga pleaded with Moggallāna to exit the "filthy" interior, Moggallāna emerged, stood between the Nāga's tusks, and used his psychic foot to strike the tusks before escaping the ensuing snap.
The Final Submission
Realizing that Moggallāna's power was absolute, Nandōpananda fled into the water, transforming into a human youth. Moggallāna, demonstrating a higher tier of Iddhī, immediately transformed into the majestic, terrifying Garuda (the ancient nemesis of the Nāga race) and pursued him. When the Nāga changed into a human, Moggallāna changed into a fierce Yakkha (Ogre) and threatened to consume him, achieving total spiritual dominance.
Defeated in every form and capacity, Nandōpananda humbled himself, confessed his profound error (Māha Mhā Chē Pyi), and took refuge in the Buddha. Moggallāna then led the converted Nāga to the Buddha, who instructed him in the Dharma, establishing him as an Upāsaka (lay follower). This decisive victory showcased that even beings of great natural power must submit to the pure, trained spiritual force of the Arahant.

lessons.title: The Eighth of the Buddha's Eight Outer Victories

formattedContent.storyteller:
This is the story of the Buddha’s eighth and final great victory over a very powerful, but mistaken, king named **Baka the Brahmā**.

**The King Who Thought He Was God**
Baka was not a human king; he was a king in the **Brahmā heaven**, a very high place. Baka was incredibly long-lived, famous, and powerful, shining like **ten suns**.

Because he lived for such a long time, Baka made a big mistake: he thought his heaven was the most permanent, wonderful, and happiest place possible, and that it would never end. He believed his heaven was the real **Nirvāṇa**, the ultimate peace.

**The Buddha's Visit**
The Buddha knew Baka was making this big, bad mistake (*Micchā Diṭṭhi*) that could harm many others. So, the Buddha went high up to the Brahmā heaven to teach Baka.

Baka welcomed the Buddha and told him, "You should live here because this place has no old age, sickness, or death! This is true happiness!".

The Buddha showed Baka his mistake by using his great wisdom and power. Baka tried to play a trick by hiding himself so the Buddha couldn't see him. But even though Baka was very powerful, the Buddha could still see him.

**The Magic Hiding**
Then the Buddha said, "Now I will hide, you try to find me!". The Buddha used his power to become **invisible** right in front of everyone. All the Brahmā kings, including Baka, could hear the Buddha’s voice talking about truth, but they could not see his body.

Baka realized the Buddha was the wisest and most powerful of all. He finally dropped his pride and admitted his mistake.

The Buddha won this final victory by using **Wisdom** to cure Baka’s wrong belief, just like medicine cures a sickness.
formattedContent.explorer:
This is the **Eighth Outer Victory of the Buddha**: the taming of **Baka the Brahmā King**. This victory was achieved by applying the **medicine of knowledge** to cure the **poison of false views**.

***

### Baka's False View of Eternity

**Baka** was a highly revered **Brahmā King** living in the **Ābhassara Brahmā realm**, which is part of the Second Jhāna heaven. He was immensely powerful, shining with great light.

Because Baka had lived for a staggering **eight *kappas*** (eons) in that realm, he developed a powerful **wrong view** (*Micchā Diṭṭhi*). He believed his life was **eternal**, that his existence was not subject to aging, sickness, or death (*Jāti, Jarā, Byādhi, Maraṇa*). He and 72 other Brahmās believed their realm was the true Nirvāṇa.

***

### The Buddha Exposes the Error

The Buddha knew that Baka's false view of **eternalism** (*Sassata Diṭṭhi*) was a dangerous obstruction for many beings. So, the Buddha traveled instantly to the Brahmā realm.

Baka, excited, welcomed the Buddha and urged him to adopt the Brahmā life, claiming it was the ultimate state of peace, free from suffering.

The Buddha immediately corrected Baka, stating that he was blind and dwelling in the "**dark realm of ignorance**" (*Avijjā*). The Buddha pointed out that Baka mistook the **impermanent** (*Anicca*) for the **permanent** (*Nicca*).

***

### The Challenge of Hiding

Baka, believing his power was equal to or greater than the Buddha’s, challenged him to a duel of psychic power.

1.  Baka attempted to use his *Iddhī* to hide his body so the Buddha could not see him.
2.  The Buddha easily saw him, proving Baka’s power was limited.
3.  The Buddha then said, "Now I will hide, you try to find me."
4.  The Buddha instantly used his power to **disappear**, but he continued to chant a verse about the danger of clinging to existence.
5.  Baka and all 72 Brahmās could hear the voice clearly, but they could **not find the invisible Buddha** anywhere.

Baka's arrogance was shattered. He admitted his mistake, and he and the 72 Brahmās abandoned their **false eternal view** and took refuge in the **Triple Gem**.
formattedContent.adventurer:
The defeat of **Baka the Brahmā King** is the **Eighth Outer Victory**. This conquest utilized the Buddha's **supreme wisdom** (*ñāṇa*) to cure a deep-seated philosophical error. The method used is called **ñāṇāgadēna vidhinā** (the method of the medicine of knowledge).

The Genesis of False Views (**Sassata Diṭṭhi** or Eternalism)

Baka’s previous lives were filled with immense merit (**Kusala**). In one life, as the hermit **Kesava**, he:
- Performed acts of great life-giving charity (**Jīvitadāna**), saving 500 merchants from the desert and protecting villagers from robbers.
- Cultivated **Jhāna** (meditative absorption) for 100,000 years.

This merit led him through increasingly shorter-lived heavens. He eventually settled in the **Ābhassara Brahmā realm** (a Second Jhāna heaven). Having lived there for an unimaginably long time (eight *kappas*), Baka could not remember his prior deaths or rebirths. He therefore concluded, along with 72 other surrounding Brahmās, that:
- Their existence was the supreme, eternal, and non-perishing ultimate reality.
- They wrongly identified this reality as **Nirvāṇa**.

The Challenge of Wisdom

The Buddha recognized the danger of this false view (**Sassata Diṭṭhi**), which prevented beings from seeking true liberation. The Buddha instantly traveled to the Brahmā realm to confront Baka.

The Buddha stated that Baka was blinded by **ignorance** (**Avijjā**) and was like a bird trapped in a cage calling to liberated beings to enter the cage. To prove his knowledge, the Buddha narrated Baka’s entire lifespan across the Brahmā realms and recounted his past great deeds as the hermit **Kesava**. This exhaustive demonstration of knowledge impressed Baka.

The Duel of Concealment

Still clinging to his pride (**Māna**), Baka challenged the Buddha to a contest of **psychic power** (**Iddhī**).

1.  Baka first attempted to use his power to become invisible to the Buddha, but the Buddha maintained continuous sight of him.
2.  The Buddha then took his turn: he instantly became invisible to all present—Baka and the 72 Brahmās. While concealed, the Buddha recited a verse summarizing the **Dharma** (about seeing danger in existence and lacking attachment). All the Brahmās could hear the profound, echoing voice but could not locate the Buddha’s physical form.

Completely defeated in knowledge and power, Baka and the 72 Brahmās praised the Buddha as the unparalleled master of the three worlds. They renounced their **Micchā Diṭṭhi** (wrong view) and vowed to follow the **Dharma**. This final conquest was achieved entirely by piercing ignorance with **supreme wisdom**.
formattedContent.voyager:
The **Conquest of Baka the Brahmā King** (*Baka Brahma-vijaya*) is the Eighth and final of the Buddha’s **Outer Victories**, a supreme triumph over the philosophical error of **eternalism** (*Sassata Diṭṭhi*) achieved by the method of **knowledge** (*ñāṇāgadēna vidhinā*).

***

### The Foundation of Baka's Error

Baka's status derived from profound **merit** (*Kusala*).
*   In a past life in Bārāṇasī, as the wealthy householder **Kesava** who became a hermit, he cultivated the **four Jhānas** (meditative absorptions).
*   He performed extraordinary acts of **life-giving charity** (*Jīvitadāna*), including conjuring a river and forest to save 500 merchants and protecting villagers from bandits.

After accruing 100,000 years of merit, Kesava was reborn through several Brahmā realms, eventually reaching the **Ābhassara Brahmā realm** (a Second Jhāna realm). Having lived there for an extremely long duration—eight *kappas*—Baka lost the ability to recall his deaths and rebirths (*Rūpa Nāma-Sutta*).

This led him to conclude that his existence was **permanent** (*Nicca*), **ultimate happiness** (*Sukha*), and exempt from the cycle of birth, decay, and death (*Jāti, Jarā, Maraṇa*). This **false view** of *Sassata Diṭṭhi* was shared by 72 other surrounding Brahmās.

***

### The Buddha's Counter-Discourse

The Buddha, residing at Jetavana, perceived the great harm of Baka's false view. He instantly traveled to the Brahmā realm and appeared visibly.

Baka welcomed the Buddha, urging him to remain, convinced that the Brahmā realm was the **ultimate refuge**. The Buddha refuted him immediately, stating that Baka was engulfed in the "**dark realm of ignorance**" (*Avijjā*) and mistook the suffering and impermanence of the realm for ultimate peace.

To shatter Baka’s chronological ignorance, the Buddha demonstrated his **omniscience** (*ñāṇa*).
*   He recited Baka's entire trajectory, stating that Baka’s total lifespan across all Brahmā realms amounted to **136,432 intermediate kappas**, still finite, and affirmed that Baka was still subject to decay and death.
*   He further recounted Baka's past great deeds as the hermit **Kesava**, proving that the Buddha knew Baka's past better than Baka knew his own past or future.

***

### The Ultimate Psychic Display (*Iddhī*)

Baka, severely humbled in knowledge, attempted to save face by challenging the Buddha to a duel of **psychic power** (*Iddhī*).

1.  **Baka's Attempt:** Baka tried to make himself invisible to the Buddha, but the Buddha maintained continuous sight of him, declaring Baka lacked the power to conceal himself.
2.  **The Buddha's Response:** The Buddha then declared, "Baka, I will now conceal myself, you search for me". The Buddha instantly used his **supreme Iddhī** to render his form completely invisible to Baka and the entire assembly. While concealed, the Buddha recited a verse about recognizing the danger in existence (*Bhava*) and the freedom from attachment. The assembly could hear the voice but could not locate the source of the sound.

Completely vanquished in both wisdom and power, Baka and the 72 Brahmās praised the Buddha as the supreme master, unique in the three worlds. They rejected their **eternalist false view** (*Micchā Diṭṭhi*), affirming the truth of the Dharma, and promised to practice accordingly. The Buddha then taught them the **Four Noble Truths** before departing.

This conquest demonstrated that **true spiritual authority** (Buddhā-wisdom) effortlessly overcomes even the mightiest arrogance and the most profound philosophical error.

***

### Analogy

**Baka the Brahmā King** was like a very old, rich prisoner in a golden cell with infinite resources. Because he had been there for millions of years, he truly believed his cell was the entire universe and his captivity was *Nirvana*. The Buddha, knowing the truth, visited the cell and did not argue philosophy, but simply used his **wisdom** (telling Baka the exact date he arrived in the cell) and his **power** (showing Baka the world outside by hiding where Baka couldn't see him) to break the illusion, proving that **liberation lay elsewhere**.

Baka's arrogance was shattered. He admitted his mistake, and he and the 72 Brahmās abandoned their false eternal view and took refuge in the Triple Gem.
content.voyager:
The conquest of Baka the Brahmā King (Baka Brahma-vijaya) is the Eighth and final of the Buddha’s Outer Victories, a supreme triumph over the philosophical error of eternalism (Sassata Diṭṭhi) achieved by the method of knowledge (ñāṇāgadēna vidhinā).
The Foundation of Baka's Error
Baka's status derived from profound Kusala (merit). In a past life in Bārāṇasī, as the wealthy householder Kesava who became a hermit, he cultivated the four Jhānas (meditative absorptions). He performed extraordinary acts of Jīvitadāna (life-giving charity), including conjuring a river and forest to save 500 merchants and protecting villagers from bandits by creating the illusion of a King and army.
After accruing 100,000 years of merit, Kesava was reborn through several Brahmā realms, eventually reaching the Ābhassara Brahmā realm (a Second Jhāna realm). Having lived there for an extremely long duration—eight kappas—Baka lost the ability to recall his deaths and rebirths (Rūpa Nāma-Sutta), leading him to conclude that his existence was permanent (Nicca), ultimate happiness (Sukha), and exempt from the cycle of birth, decay, and death (Jāti, Jarā, Maraṇa). This false view of Sassata Diṭṭhi was shared by 72 other surrounding Brahmās.
The Buddha's Counter-Discourse
The Buddha, residing at Jetavana, perceived the great harm of Baka's false view. He instantly traveled to the Brahmā realm and appeared visibly.
Baka welcomed the Buddha, urging him to remain, convinced that the Brahmā realm was the ultimate refuge. The Buddha refuted him immediately, stating that Baka was engulfed in the "dark realm of ignorance" (Avijjā) and mistook the suffering and impermanence of the realm for ultimate peace.
To shatter Baka’s chronological ignorance, the Buddha demonstrated his omniscience (ñāṇa). He recited Baka's entire trajectory, stating that Baka’s total lifespan across all Brahmā realms amounted to 136,432 intermediate kappas, still finite, and affirmed that Baka was still subject to decay and death. He further recounted Baka's past great deeds as the hermit Kesava, proving that the Buddha knew Baka's past better than Baka knew his own past or future.
The Ultimate Psychic Display (Iddhī)
Baka, severely humbled in knowledge, attempted to save face by challenging the Buddha to a duel of psychic power (Iddhī).
1. Baka's Attempt: Baka tried to make himself invisible to the Buddha, but the Buddha maintained continuous sight of him, declaring Baka lacked the power to conceal himself.
2. The Buddha's Response: The Buddha then declared, "Baka, I will now conceal myself, you search for me". The Buddha instantly used his supreme Iddhī to render his form completely invisible to Baka and the entire assembly. While concealed, the Buddha recited a verse about recognizing the danger in existence (Bhava) and the freedom from attachment. The assembly could hear the voice but could not locate the source of the sound.
Completely vanquished in both wisdom and power, Baka and the 72 Brahmās praised the Buddha as the supreme master, unique in the three worlds. They rejected their eternalist false view (Micchā Diṭṭhi), affirming the truth of the Dharma, and promised to practice accordingly. The Buddha then taught them the Four Noble Truths before departing.
This conquest demonstrated that true spiritual authority (Buddhā-wisdom) effortlessly overcomes even the mightiest arrogance and the most profound philosophical error.
Analogy: Baka the Brahmā King was like a very old, rich prisoner in a golden cell with infinite resources. Because he had been there for millions of years, he truly believed his cell was the entire universe and his captivity was Nirvana. The Buddha, knowing the truth, visited the cell and did not argue philosophy, but simply used his wisdom (telling Baka the exact date he arrived in the cell) and his power (showing Baka the world outside by hiding where Baka couldn't see him) to break the illusion, proving that liberation lay elsewhere.

This is the story of the Buddha’s eighth and final great victory over a very powerful, but mistaken, king named Baka the Brahmā.
The King Who Thought He Was God
Baka was not a human king; he was a king in the Brahmā heaven, a very high place. Baka was incredibly long-lived, famous, and powerful, shining like ten suns.
Because he lived for such a long time, Baka made a big mistake: he thought his heaven was the most permanent, wonderful, and happiest place possible, and that it would never end. He believed his heaven was the real Nirvāṇa, the ultimate peace.
The Buddha's Visit
The Buddha knew Baka was making this big, bad mistake (Micchā Diṭṭhi) that could harm many others. So, the Buddha went high up to the Brahmā heaven to teach Baka.
Baka welcomed the Buddha and told him, "You should live here because this place has no old age, sickness, or death! This is true happiness!".
The Buddha showed Baka his mistake by using his great wisdom and power. Baka tried to play a trick by hiding himself so the Buddha couldn't see him. But even though Baka was very powerful, the Buddha could still see him.
The Magic Hiding
Then the Buddha said, "Now I will hide, you try to find me!". The Buddha used his power to become invisible right in front of everyone. All the Brahmā kings, including Baka, could hear the Buddha’s voice talking about truth, but they could not see his body.
Baka realized the Buddha was the wisest and most powerful of all. He finally dropped his pride and admitted his mistake.
The Buddha won this final victory by using Wisdom to cure Baka’s wrong belief, just like medicine cures a sickness.
